analysis.one_liner: Requires ballistics testing of the 50 gun models most used in crime, to trace bullets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee in April 2000 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury to publish an annual list of the 50 firearms most frequently used in crimes. Manufacturers and importers of those guns would then have to test-fire each gun before selling it, record the unique markings it leaves on bullets and casings, and feed those records into a national computer database that police could use to match crime-scene evidence to a gun. Gun makers who skipped the testing could face fines up to $20,000 or suspension or loss of their federal license [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people affected by gun crime. Ballistics records let investigators match a bullet or casing found at a crime scene to the specific gun that fired it, helping identify shooters and solve shootings. The bill also directed annual reports on how many investigations and prosecutions used these records [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have created a national database of ballistics records for the most crime-prone guns, letting investigators match crime-scene evidence to the exact firearm and trace it [S2] [S3].
The top-50 list would have been published annually in the Federal Register, focusing tracing on the models criminals actually use [S2].
The bill directed the Attorney General and Treasury to give manufacturers government ballistics equipment, training, and technical help so the testing could be done at manufacturer sites [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Licensed firearms manufacturers and importers whose models make the crime list. They would bear the cost of test-firing, record-keeping, and database compliance, and risk civil fines up to $20,000 or suspension or revocation of their license for violations [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Only the 50 most crime-used models would be covered, so many guns used in crimes would escape tracing; the list could also shift as criminals switch to unlisted models [S2].

The bill limited judicial review of the Treasury's enforcement actions to the existing section 923(f) process, which gun makers and their allies could argue gave the agency too much power over licensees [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the compliance burden: smaller manufacturers would need government-supplied equipment and training just to keep selling listed models [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people endangered by gun violence, the benefit—faster identification of guns used in shootings—is real, though modest, because the requirement covers only the 50 most crime-used models. The cost falls narrowly on licensed manufacturers and importers in the form of testing and record-keeping, cushioned by the bill's own promise of government equipment and training. On paper the trade favors the public; the bill simply never got far enough for the trade to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2000, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and then to its Crime Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Xavier Becerra introduced the Bullet Tracing Act on April 3, 2000 [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Crime [S5].
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors during its lifetime [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and importers, who avoided new test-firing, record-keeping, and licensing risk, while communities waiting on improved gun-crime tracing got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms makers avoided new tracing rules

for.name: Rep. Xavier Becerra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never took it up; it never reached a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 7, 2000 and held no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of any potential support or opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.note: They would have to test-fire listed models, keep ballistics records, and risk fines up to $20,000 or license suspension or revocation. The records would help police trace crime guns, a public benefit the industry's compliance costs would fund. [S2] [S3]
